Almost every review that tries to go into detail starts with 'this game is like...' and ends with 'but that's okay because...' and I want to offer a slightly different perspective. Not having played other survival horror games, I didn't actually recognize many of the references or influences others talk about while I was playing. Even the references to books and anime that I was familiar with managed to just kind of lull in the background, like the classical music that plays over certain areas - something that was familiar, that I recognized, but which was clearly being used for a purpose wholly original to this game, this story.

So I want to talk about what it felt like to play this game on its own terms.

It is a game whose story and gameplay are merged. Everything you do in the game ties back to some aspect of the story and every part of the story has a connection to how you play. The setting is used to explain gameplay mechanics, like only having six item slots, as well as the many puzzles littered throughout the game. The story itself is a downward progression into terrible, hard to accept truths, and the increasing intensity of gameplay mirrors your character journey in a way that makes the story more accessible. As you scrounge around, making tough decisions - do I use my ammo, to free up inventory space? Should I carry healing items with me? Should I use my healing items now, or save them? Should I kill these zombies, knowing they might come back, or do i just try to sneak past every time? - you find yourself more and more immersed in the game, in its story and characters, even as actual information is sparse. 

Little gameplay elements reinforce all of this very neatly; for example, you are always painfully aware of exactly how much ammo you have and how many inventory slots are open. However, you do not have concrete numbers for how much damage your attacks deal, or how much damage you take in a given hit. There are ways to suss it out that become clear as you play for longer, but you can never really take for granted that it will only take two bullets to take down this enemy, or that you have X number of hits you can take before you're in danger. So, you always feel a bit risky, a bit on edge, and that feeling bleeds over into the story the game is telling very nicely.

Once you get further in, you finally start to get answers to some (not all) of your questions, and now your mind is just on fire and you start make up your own answers to some of the things left unsaid. Now you're really rolling, you want to see how it ends but the difficulty has started to spike so now you start to take risks and say 'yes, I will spend all of my ammo to clear this room, even if they might come back' or 'yes I think I can get across this whole route with no healing items on me because I need an inventory slot open for that thing.' You start to use unfamiliar weapons because the ones you know are out of ammo, and this creates new emergent gameplay, as well as teaching you rules you maybe weren't aware of, like how some enemies take more or less damage from some weapon types. You make mistakes, firing too early and missing, trying to run past something but missing your timing and taking a hit, but you power through, its not worth going back and loading a save, you want to get to the end of the story.
And then, eventually, you do. And its worth the work you put in.

I am currently considering taking a second run. I think I will give the game's story, which is quite dense and rich, time for my mind to digest it before I jump back in. But I expect I will jump back in. This game is just such a feast, such a beautiful wedding of story and gameplay, such a strong argument for how mechanics affect mood and mood affects story. It's just really good, folks; it is intense and dark and creepy and sad and really, really good.

Signalis was pitched to me by its fandom and some friends of mine as something very simple. "Lesbian robot game". This is entirely true, this game is about lesbian love and robots. But this oversimplification was a trap to get me into a very existential game. 

The game itself is a love story. And a love letter to its genre and themes. Subliminal, vague, obscene, absurd, at times engrossingly underwritten, overwritten in small moments but with resounding resonance to the rest of the plot. There is nothing imperfect about this game in its aesthetic or tone or story telling, nor its music. However, it does pay tribute to classic survival horror in a way that those of little patience may feel a disconnect. I played the game with classic settings and tank controls, only to vow that I never will again. That being said, even with extra slots for the pick ups on certain modes, this game relentlessly sticks to its rules and you will have to play by them no matter what.

Gameplay wise, its one of the best of its type and the puzzles are challenging enough to take some consideration, but not too overly hard to be frustrating. Those without a stomach for puzzle-driven games and back-tracking may turn away, but I suggest you suffer through the trials to experience more of the plot.

The game is great at telling its story by not telling it much at all. Unwritten words and suggestions ironically make vague sentences all the more impactful. Like a child being raised in a politicized and militant society, its mechanics and lore are written in-universe by the environment itself. What most games would tell in a text prompt or overly long tutorial, the game tells you in the form of posters and propaganda pamphlets. However, in true survival horror and Dead Space fashion (which this game borrows a lot from narratively and thematically, as well as visually) there is a literal note telling you in all caps how to defeat most enemies. Its still far from as belittling as the original Dead Space was.

The game borrows a lot from many things, from the works of Nihei Tsutomu and to some very good literature, yet it has its own identity. So many games that evoke nostalgic feelings for an otherwise dead genre (starting to see how this plays into the game more than ever...) simply appropriate visuals and not much more. But the fidelity and artistic vision of the game is not at all restricted by its PS1 graphics, only enhanced. The gameplay is fine tuned, the animations are great, the sounds, the soundtrack, everything about this game is really superior to most horror developed by larger studios. 

It also does what E.Y.E Divine Cybermancy tried to do with loops and the cycles of guilt far better, I must admit. E.Y.E clearly appropriated many things to the point of it being a near plagarization of its inspirations, its deepest concepts lifted straight from various philosophical sources and belief systems. This is best emphasized by the fact that so many characters share distorted names taken from their sources of inspiration. 

A lot of E.Y.E's charm was what was lost in translation, was gained in humour and unique flow of text, as well as accidentally becoming esoteric and surreal, due to how the machine translation fumbled high brow concepts into some very unfriendly language. 

Signalis is the opposite of that. It is a boldly inspired game, but entirely unique to itself and doesn't rely so heavily on the references as one may think. A scene otherwise identical to a part in Ghost in the Shell is in fact very narratively significant to the plot and has been more than just appropriated into the story, it has been implanted and made its own. Much like how ELSTER implants limbs from other units onto herself. Much like how Replikas draw from neural databanks of humans and at times, they emulate needs of organic bodies that their synthetic ones do not need. And if they allow themselves to not indulge in these niches, they become distraught. Signalis acknowledges that its mandatory to pay tribute to its cultural benefactors to not fall apart, but it is not entirely the sum of a bunch of things sewn together like E.Y.E was. Which is ironic, the more you understand what happens in the story...

Signalis is not lost in translation, its deliberately not even fully transliterated in its unique Chinese-East German inspired aesthetic. Signalis (Esperanto for "Signal") is a transmission of dissonant waves that only share a conscious existence in being sound that can be interpreted, intercepted through static. And the fandom has done some spectacular explorations with the setting it was given from this game. In times where large copyright holders hold modern myth and folklore, smaller games like this bring out the artisans in others. Its not a product, its players not consumers. Its art and its open to interpretation, both destructive and constructive. 

When I finished the first game, I immediately started a new run to get the secret ending. During this time, two things happened.

A childhood friend of mine died of a lingering illness. As in, they were actively dying and yet, they were living through this process until the very end. If there is one thing that this game reminded me of, which also deals with a similar concept in physical and metaphysical, metaphorical ways - it is that once death arrives, dying is already over. The fragility of life is tragic and with that, there is at least peace in times knowing that the broken no longer have to hold themselves together.

A second thing, the fandom effectively had a Cold War that no one knew about until it was too late. Yuri-horror fans vs the military factions that enjoyed the whole 200 words of exploration about the distant war. In the end, both parties more or less shook hands and walked away. It was mockingly called the "Checkpoint Charlie" incident of the fandom, a reference to when tank-build up by Soviets and Americans in East Germany nearly caused a genuine conflict but was ultimately talked down by mutual, sensible discussion between the world leaders of the then-superpowers. 

My personal take is that the war and the background themes of the game, while the fixation of some parts of the playerbase, merely existed to align with a certain other Chinese-characteristic of the plot itself. That being, the Mandate of Heaven.

The matriarchal rebels of Rotfront and the Eusan nation have lost the Mandate of Heaven. In Chinese history, the Mandate of Heaven is lost when there is dissatisfaction/rebellion, disease and epidemics, as well as famine. 

The revolutionary Eusans were rebels that broke away from the Empire. The Empire, in turn, has enforced a blockade that has pushed a planet into starvation. And finally, everyone is sick and puking blood. 

These themes merely isolate the stakes of everything into an individual level (even though the characters themselves may represent collectives of people in the system or even collectives of thoughts and dreams and experiences forcefully bound to one person) by further decaying the world they exist in around them in real time. Exemplified more by Elster's reactions to the National Flag in the late game. Either way, this puts things in perspective in more ways than one.

Going back to the loss of my friend, when you lose someone suddenly - you realize how much you could have been there. And you imagine if you had even one more day, even if everything was going to be in hell, you'd take it.

That is what Signalis and its secret ending, meant to me. 

The world is ending and the walls closed in, rather than fell down. 

And all you want is one more moment.

The absence of something makes us appreciate what was once there.

Greatest of all time. Zenith of the medium. Hallmark of media. Gold standard of storytelling. Apogee of creativity. Vertex of invention. Crest of ingenuity. Acme of imagination. Pinnacle of innovation. Epic of epics. Legend among legends. Peak fiction. Sesbian Lex.

SIGNALIS applies a classic mix of German and Japanese to its oldschool anime aesthetics reminiscent of Ghost in the Shell. It's a sombre sci-fi full of loving homages to Lovecraft, shivering monstrosities from Silent Hill, and System Shock's synthetic horror of self. It draws from many playbooks, but there's no unerring formula holding it together. Dedication is the only adhesive, the rest is ether. Prepare to get spellbound by a backtracking-intensive contraption performing on par with Resident Evil. Extending game-wide, a captivating logistical loop at the base of all mechanics magnifies your perception of places and things, being a philosopher's stone that turns scarcity and nuisances into high-class entertainment, a romance of desperation and ruin.

[h3]Flavour[/h3]
To start with the little things, the UI is great, especially the map that you can rely on. Until you can't. For controls, I used keyboard and mouse, which lend themselves to the task perfectly, making the game feel like an intentionally handicapped SHMUP. The default keybinds actually make sense, imagine that! I liked the look of the CRT filter, too bad it also makes fonts barely readable. But the mix of high definition and crunchy pixels is appealing without enhancers. Cute touches like visual glitches make it seem like the world is torn at the seams while lo-fi POV sequences give off a vibe of a VHS Horror game. Isometric landscapes aren't that varied or picturesque, but crispy shadows playing in the lights as well as striking colour accents of kitschy propaganda posters liven things up.

The levels themselves are well-structured, sporting complex looping layouts. To cruise their depths, you take control of a sophisticated android, or Replika, named Elster. She's looking for a woman, her ex-commander, in the mines and corporate infrastructure around them on the planet Leng situated on the outskirts of a system inhabited by the nation of Eusan. Their "wonderful Nation" is at war with the Empire. None of these sides is a light side, it's more of a Sadako vs. Kayako engagement. Eusan's regime used to be monstrous long before its subjects turned into ones. Cameras all over the place follow you silently, enforcing the feeling of being under ever-present totalitarian surveillance. You'll find all the lore in pompous pamphlets and sad diaries, most of which are censored in one way or another. It's a joy to get familiar with, the precise writing delivers a world of misery to your doorstep.

The game starts building its unsettling world subtly even before introducing its first enemy, quietly slipping under your skin. You'll be soaking in contemplative cutscenes and bits of dialogue with rare characters, their tone ranging from melancholic to desperate. Going up against a devastated world of mad cyborgs, you can barely see what they represent visually. Just silhouettes of shivering horrors in the dark. Listen, let the sharp sound design complete the picture in your mind instead. It goes hard. From unnervingly quiet ambience to demonic screeching. The musical score is used sparsely to emphasise special moments and incite terror during combat encounters by blowing your ear drums out your ass. The shots shrill and the hits rip. It's satisfying to end their pain. Yours persists.

[h3]Inventory Horror[/h3]
The real headache is deciding what to do with droves of different puzzle components taking up inventory space. Make sure to always have at least a couple of slots open for them. Puzzle-solving itself won't take much of your time or brain energy, yet it infallibly serves as a solid incentive to progress through the game. Local brain-teasers perfectly fit the genre's standards by not being too dastard or insultingly easy, keeping the tradition of mostly revolving around collecting stuff to slide into slots. SIGNALIS has struck a balance here, all that decision-making and problem-solving beget gratification. Another good design is the way it gives you gameplay hints, masquerading helpful advice as propaganda. Like that "no running in the hallways" poster telling you to be sneaky.

It goes further than that. The Rule of Six, one of the in-game laws, says that you can carry no more than 6 items on you, justifying a mechanic while showing private property as a privilege. This severe limitation can be remedied. Consider stepping into the unknown territory surveillance, don't drag health items and surplus ammo around, never hope to grab everything in one go. Dedicate separate runs with an empty bag to snatching everything that isn't nailed down and hauling it back to a save room. These greed trips that can go very wrong are part of the fun. Also, saving is free, so nobody stops you from abusing it. I admit that it dilutes the spiciness coming from gambling with your life, but the thrill of potentially losing a chunk of progress to the monstrosities still remains.

[h3]Trigger Discipline[/h3]
Those are rather slow, although, they strike rapidly and have a long reach, so it isn't easy to just avoid or bait their attacks. Elster can't evade fast and gets easily cornered in cramped spaces. She pushes nearby enemies away, but it does little when they're piling on her. However, screwing up is seldom lethal, our girl is made of titanium. And she's packing. Pistol, SMG, shotgun, rifle, revolver, a grenade-launching flare gun. All the classics. Ammo isn't even that scarce but killing is a temporary measure since enemies get up after a while. It's a long while, but this constant threat makes you think strategically, teaching to stay low and pick your fights. You can also use thermite to dispose of the most annoying corpses for good. These are rare moments of solidifying dominance and establishing a semblance of permanence. Burn, baby, burn.

To ensure that its convictions are feasible, SIGNALIS introduces an effective, if rudimentary, stealth system. If you keep your distance, you can slowly walk by the monsters when they're turned away. It's a reliable mechanic unless you get cocky. Clinging to the wall, you can sneak past that neighbour's poodle for years, it's all bark and no bite. But you know these bastards, one day it's gonna go crazy and try to taste your flesh. Similarly, here you may walk back and forth unnoticed forever, but forget to turn the flashlight off just once and get chased by a crowd of eldritch androids while running low on ammo, then jump into a hole and get rekt by a boss. But this is probably the only way for one to kill you, those are easy when you catch on to their gimmicks.

Past the early game, I caught on to the game's Zen flow. Don't try to have it all, don't jump into holes unprepared, don't kill if you don't have to. My victims were the ones patrolling narrow passages or places I had to visit often. The rest gave me enough room to slip by. One can go through the whole thing with a minuscule body count. I spent my resources quite frivolously and wasted tons of ammo and health in panic romps, yet I was still left with some to spare at the end. Thus, I disagree with anyone claiming that the game doesn't provide enough sustenance. You should've seen my collection of healing sprays alone! But even when I died, losing progress, to circle back around more efficiently felt rewarding.

[h3]Last Words[/h3]
The same can be said about my experience at large. SIGNALIS is cyberpunk, biopunk... all the punks! Whatever happens, a strong underlying message of non-conformity is always present. The plot begins intentionally obfuscated but doesn't leave you hanging. It's an emotional story that eventually becomes crystal clear, at least after one of the normal endings I got. Akin to their counterparts in Silent Hill, each ending provides closure, albeit with a different aftertaste. "Taste" is the word here. Playing a game created by true connoisseurs of the genre was an exquisite treat.

Wow. Just wow. SIGNALIS is less of a proper game than it is a twisted, nightmarish art piece. No other game, no other story even, has made me feel the way SIGNALIS did. It is melancholic joy made manifest, run through with a generous helping of existential terror. The art, the atmosphere, the soundtrack, the writing, and the meticulous design of every puzzle and environment are some of my absolute favourites. 

SIGNALIS is an isometric survival horror game, inspired by the classics of the genre such as Resident Evil and Silent Hill. In it, you play as a Replika (biomechanical android) named LSTR-512 (Elster), who is searching for a woman named Alina. On her journey, it becomes apparent that not everything is as it initially seemed, and I feel that to elaborate on that point any further would cheapen the experience. The gameplay is mildly challenging, especially for those not accustomed to the genre. Limited inventory, clunky combat, intrusive interaction windows, and unreliably spongy enemies may certainly become points of frustration for those used to a cleaner, more modern gameplay experience, but PLEASE do not let that dissuade you from trying the game.

If you have even a remote interest in sci-fi/psychological horror, SIGNALIS is absolute gem of a game packed with mystery, suspense, philosophy and metaphysics, and much more. Easily one of my favourite games of all time. Kudos to rose-engine and the rest of the team for crafting a truly unforgettable experience.

I heard about Signalis when I saw it described as "lesbian robots being sad". As a fan of the original Silent Hill, I was definitely drawn to the retro, rough-hewn PS1-style graphics, reality-bending motifs, and themes on death, life, radios, and liminality. 

As a retro horror game, Signalis succeeds. The music is excellent. The game can be enjoyed on a pretty basic level, where you run around a confusing dark setting with limited inventory space and solve clunky puzzles. There was a middle-section where the game almost lost me, as I thought "oh here we go, another horror game disappearing up its own ass!" However...

...Like the symbol seen on the title page, this onion has layers. 

As an exploration of psychological themes and dreams, Signalis succeeds. As a bonkers sad robot lesbian anime game, Signalis succeeds. As an alternative-world science-fiction exploration on facism, war, labor, and human/android rights, Signalis succeeds. For fans of Taoism, the Hero's Journey, German art, classic literature, Signalis succeeds. I can't guarantee this game is for you, but it does contain a little something for everyone; an overall message on the meaning of life in a walnut-y package... it cannot be swallowed whole, but must be carefully picked apart and thoughtfully chewed. 

I finished the game and stewed on it for a couple days, and I expect to return to it to try to get a different ending, but I may not replay the whole thing. [h1]A Cult Classic in the making[/h1]

When I first played SIGNALIS, it was approximately 2 or 3 months out already. I had anticipated it before release. Looking at its store page, a unique indie title that seemed to promise a deviation, some interesting gameplay, cool character and level design, I would’ve never guessed I was about to play a game that will comfortably enthrone itself among the greatest horror games, and even among the greatest games period. 

It has been one of the most evocative video games I have experienced, and easily my game of the year for 2022. Start to finish, this game feels like one of the rare instances where a video game ascends far beyond its compatriots, and is an article worthy of mention as one of the greatest creations of this medium.

[b]The short and simple[/b]

SIGNALIS is an isometric horror-survival game, consisting of linear levels that grow iteratively until the player unlocks the next level.

[h1]What makes this game perfect?[/h1]

The game has 3 core elements that encapsulate it;

[b]Atmosphere[/b]

Perhaps one of the strongest overarching and gripping elements of SIGNALIS is a nearly unparalleled vibe throughout the game, informed by a unique idea for a setting; the world of the game is oppressive, melancholic, and at the same time so inviting. The dilapidated state of it, astride reality and paranormality, is a feast for the senses, and has left me completely perplexed how such audiovisual richness have been achieved by a development team of two people.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2942492378


[b]Gameplay[/b]

The gameplay of SIGNALIS is intertwined with its atmosphere, in that sense it can be viewed as an extension of the above paragraph. Horror survival gameplay is not easy to nail, and enthusiasts of this genre will not be surprised to find a lot of ‘horror’ games foregoing the whole “survival” bit because the mundanity of combat that can often be witnessed in this genre. I’ve always had the opinion that combat in horror survival games is more defined by how it looks and feels, rather than how it plays. It is less about mechanics and quantified gameplay, and more about solidifying the feel of trying to survive in lethal situations. “Game logic” can sometimes be fatal to games where atmosphere is the main driving point. While Silent Hill 2 has always been one of my favourite games, I will never spare an opportunity to vehemently criticize how jarring and dissonant its fighting was. Signalis is to me is only perhaps paralleled by The Evil Within in terms of combat. It has less weapons and “mechanics” to be sure, but the acoustics, the recoil, the feedback, the graphical elements are rarely eclipsed. Firing a grenade in a dark room full of monsters and watching the muzzle flash and subsequent explosion light up the entire room for a split second before the darkness sets back in is one of the many scenarios that have elicited me to shower this game with praise.

Aside from the combat, the game is truly deviant with its gameplay. You will find yourself learning basic cryptology to solve some puzzles, and maybe you will even end up educating yourself on radios during or after finishing this game. The game features a good deal of puzzles, all of which were unique and interesting to go through. It has succeeded in remaining fresh to me, in its entire length, and each time I was not playing it was time spent anticipating playing it to get to the next narrative beat or understand a little more of its phantasm-like story.

There can be a lot of backtracking in the game due to its very small size inventory. I admit, I did an insane amount of backtracking myself, because my Elster either carried to much or too little, but I was so enthralled by the journey that not a single moment of tedium was to be found in all of this. In my 2nd and 3rd playthroughs I had not had any trouble with this, though. 

Much like other horror games, SIGNALIS has numerous endings, some with esoteric requirements – as is tradition in the genre.

[b]Narrative (?)[/b]

Definition of ‘Narrative’, per google;
[i]“a spoken or written account of connected events; a story”[/i]

SIGNALIS does not have a conventional narrative. It has a sequence of events, but they proceed in a weird and hazy state, lending the game the countenance of a fever dream. Over the course of the game, everything looks so familiar, and many sights will elicit a both the sense of Déjà vu or Jamais vu constantly. To this day, there is no one universally accepted conjecture on what it all means. Everything feels like a fleeting mirage and an apparition, and every time a connection is found, it reveals even more threads. The story of the game feels like everything is loosely connected and at the same time disconnected that it’s a struggle to describe it. 

[b]Art[/b]

I will dedicate this paragraph to one of the most sensational experiences I had with any game; the game features a lot of classical music, a true treat, but nothing comes close to running through the dimly lit halls of Sierpinski while listening to Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake. Moment after moment in this game spellbound me, and fanned my passion towards it.

[b]Conclusion;[/b]

This is what an article of media looks like when it is created with grace, refinement and passion. Horror survival in recent years seems to be more or less lacking, with many games taking the cheapest route towards scaring the player, or indulge in dull clichés like zombies. This game has ascended well and far above. It’s unique, special, and worthy of being celebrated.

[quote] SIGNALIS is legitimately one of the best classic survival horror games to come out in recent times. If you’re interested in the genre, take a look at this title! [/quote]

Recently, a bunch of people on my twitter feed started raving about a game. “One of the best indie survival horror games in a long time”, they said. “Really good stuff”, some added. “I’d give away a family member to be able to erase this from my mind and replay it”, one exclaimed. That last one went a bit too far and I can’t say I’d go there with him, but I fully agree with the other two statements. [b]SIGNALIS is really good.[/b] Read on and you’ll hopefully understand why I think so. [b]And don’t worry: this review is spoiler-free![/b]

[b]SIGNALIS is a classic survival horror experience.[/b] Think an experience rooted in ps1/ps2 era games such as resident evil and silent hill. The game borrows a lot from those and other titles, and is all the better for it - starting with its gameplay.

[b]The game is played from an isometric/third-person perspective.[/b] You play as Elster, “a technicial Replika searching for her lost dreams”, according to the developer in the steam store page. In SIGNALIS, you walk through multiple similar-looking but very different sci-fi settings, such as crashed spaceships and stations riddled with enemies. You have the abilities you would expect from games of the genre: you can walk, sprint, interact with things and shoot. And you’ll be doing a lot of all of these things. In some occasions, you’ll also be swapped to first person mode - but these modes are very basic, and only include walking and/or interacting with things, and they usually don’t last long.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2885938032

[b]True to the originals of the genre, this game has a lot of puzzles.[/b] In fact, it would not be an understatement to say the game is mostly divided into a few different sections. You have to complete all the puzzles in one section, which then permanently puts you in the next. These sections can be big, spanning multiple floors and dozens of different rooms. This might be a bit of a dejavu for you, but you’ll spend most of your time hunting for keys. Most often, one room will have a solution to a puzzle in another room, which will then give you a key to a corridor, which will lead you to places that have other items you need, so on, so forth. [b]Needless to say, this game involves a lot of backtracking… but not just because of the puzzles.[/b]

[b]One BIG element here is that you need to think about your actions. The entire game is designed with that in mind.[/b] You can only carry 6 items in your inventory, which means that you’ll either often be backtracking to store stuff, or have to dump potentially important resources such as health or ammo just so you have one extra slot available to spend a bit more time exploring. Sometimes, both situations will be the case at the same time. Furthermore, the game gives you limited resources in terms of ammo, but it throws a LOT of enemies in your path. What all this means is: you have to think about which items you want to bring, and you have to think about which enemies you want to kill, or which ones you just want to avoid. The actual shooting part is tight, and the game has a variety of your good old standard weapons available for use.

[b]But while the gameplay is good, I think SIGNALIS’ biggest strength definitely lies in its setting.[/b] The sci-fi and mysterious world the developers created is amazing, and it was honestly all a delight to see. From bases in multiple planets and crashed spaceships to android-like fully sentient beings and other things we can only dream of one day having in real life (...or not), SIGNALIS has it all, and it also nails it all. [b]The setting is also further, and masterfully, complemented by both the soundtrack and the visuals of the game.[/b]

The soundtrack is mostly ambient, aside from a song that plays every time an enemy spots you, but that all just makes you appreciate the actual tracks a lot more when they happen, as it’s usually in emotional moments that hit you like a truck. The visuals are what you see on the pictures and videos in the steam store page: PS1 style… but I can not stress this enough: they are absolutely GORGEOUS! I mean, just look at this picture I took in one of the cutscenes.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2885937763

But there is one more important aspect in SIGNALIS that I haven’t even begun to mention: its horror elements. The game is marketed, after all, as a survival horror game, so how does it fare in that regard? Well, in my opinion, it fares great, but it’s important to note that [b]this isn’t a scary experience[/b] - or at least, it wasn’t for me. The game doesn’t try to scare you, especially not with cheap tactics such as jumpscares (which might still happen anyway if you’re all tensed up trying to sneak around an enemy, get spotted and hear their shriek). Instead, [b]the horror elements here lie again in its setting, its theme, the aesthetic, and perhaps most importantly, both the tension and the overall creep factor of some elements, especially some cutscenes.[/b] If you’re anything like me as a player, you’ll always be feeling on edge as you try to preserve your resources and not die to the lots of monsters with genuinely disturbing designs. And the designs are pretty varied! So, even if it doesn’t try to scare you, the game does nail its horror elements.

[b]That being said, SIGNALIS isn’t without its issues.[/b] But then again, what is in life? First point that might annoy some is related to the inventory and back tracking. While it is a design decision, I know some people won’t be too excited about having to so carefully control what they carry, and be stopped from picking up items they need because they have no space. And while we’re talking about design, the game could use potentially more variety in terms of monsters. There are lots of different designs, mind you, and the few boss fights that are there are pretty fun, even if gimmicky, but quite a few of the designs just walk up to you and try to melee you. One of my favorite enemies was one that required the radio to beat, mainly because it was the one that mostly changed the dynamic with the enemy. The first person sections are also very basic. It’s sometimes unclear what you can click when you’re on point and click mode, and you move very slowly on walking simulator sections, with no possibility to sprint. These are all nitpicks compared to the overall quality of the game, but I still figured I needed to mention them. In fact, the only glitch I ran into was in a walking simulator section. I basically had to set my radio to a specific frequency and then click on a lock, but every time I clicked on the lock with the right frequency, it didn’t work. I was going nuts until it randomly worked without me actually changing anything. This glitch aside, the game ran pretty well for me, no other technical problems found!

[b]All in all, I actually am a massive fan of this game.[/b] I hope this review helped shed some light onto why exactly I enjoyed it so much, but if not, or if you have any questions, remember that I’m always up to chat! If you do pick up SIGNALIS, I hope you enjoy it!

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Wake up...wake up. I haven't felt as stressed and anxious playing a game as I did with Signalis. Despite not having jumpscares or scary foes, this survival horror game manages to disturb me with its setting alone. Signalis is a game that came out in 2022. It surprised players with its atmosphere, gameplay, and plot—a love letter to the classic survival horror of the 90s.

[h1] Control and Gameplay [/h1]
The controls in Signalis are reminiscent of the classic Resident Evil games. The camera has a fixed angle, and you control the character with the analog; you point, shoot, and reload weapons. Puzzles are rewarding to solve, as the title doesn't hold the player's hand and requires thoughtful exploration to crack them and unlock new areas and weapons.

The game balance is excellent, as you need to conserve ammo to succeed and know when to engage in combat or use stealth to save resources. Fallen enemies can rise again, giving another layer to deciding when to eliminate enemies. For example, you frequent a hallway too much to move around the area. In that case, it might be intelligent to dispatch the enemies, even temporarily. Down the line, there is the option to remove some foes permanently, but only occasionally.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2964296074

The only bad thing I found with the title is the inventory space. I know this is a common complaint among players. Still, in a game where you must move with six key items simultaneously multiple times while having only six slots in the inventory, that is an issue. There were numerous times when I was forced to backtrack forcibly to get my weapon and equipment back. It can be particularly infuriating when there are multiple enemies in hallways that get blocked, resulting in taking almost mandatory damage. 

[h1] Graphics[/h1]
The game was tested with an RTX 2060, 36 GB of ram, Intel Core i7-11700K - Core i7 11th Gen Rocket Lake 8-Core 3.6 GHz LGA 1200. The game ran at +60 FPS with no issues.

Signalis graphics are not the best; they are similar to Playstation 1 graphics, if anything. However, what it lacks in graphics, it makes up in ambiance, for the title sets up a gritty, suffocating atmosphere that pulls you right into it. The clever use of dark areas only being explorable with a flashlight, using the radio to discover clues/survive foes, or even changing into first person camera all show that Signalis always have an ace in the deck to both surprise and spook the player.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2964293314

[h1] Sound[/h1]
The sound of Signalis only makes the experience more terrific! Enemies can scream as they die, some foes can be outright disturbing when you walk into a room, and there is something heavy about listening to the monsters approaching you. The game lacks voice acting, but with the nature and details of the sound effects, there is no need for it.

Weapons leave a loud bang as they shoot, sucking out all the sound, and listening carefully can hint at what might be lurking in the shadows. Weapon effects are so crips that they could even rival AAA games; the sound of the shooting is insanely good, especially with headsets! 

The music also adds an unsettling feeling to the areas, and during combat, it elevates the anxiety of the situation. There are many genres here, from classic to outright disturbing. If you like science fiction and horror, you will feel right at home. The games' tracks are not original to the title, but they are authentic pieces of music, like how The Evil Within uses Clair De Lune.

[h1] Story and Characters [/h1]
You play LSTR-512, also known as Elster, an android that finds herself in a shipwreck on a planet missing her human officer. As Elster explores the world, she discovers that not everything is what it seems and that some infection is going around. She will witness atrocities and abominations while searching for the missing human.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2964293089

I cannot go into details without doing a massive disservice to Signalis, it is a game that you should play blind, so it is sort of hard to go into more information. How the story plays out and what you get from it is up to you, the player, as you explore the rooms and environments, collecting pieces of lore that will give you hints of what is happening behind sinister layers.

For such a short game, it made me care about some of the characters in the story. My favorite one is Isolde Itou, as she grew on me and had some excellent interactions with the main character. Meeting NPC and trying to get a feel for who they are, why they are in this situation, and what will become of them is interesting.

[h1] Replayability [/h1]
The game has some replayability, with multiple endings that could deserve another run. Each run can take 6 to 12 hours, depending on how you tackle the game, and each conclusion requires its run to be achieved. Signalis will be something you beat once and be done with it for most players, but for those who want to complete it to 100%, it can quickly get to 20 to 40 hours. 

[h1] Conclusion[/h1]
Signalis is an incredible survival horror game and one of the best games of 2022; as a player, do yourself a favor and buy it as it only costs 20 bucks and is a genre masterpiece. I don't need to sell you on this one; is that good. A clever game that knows how to adapt the visuals and environments into the gameplay, along with a unique atmosphere that makes the air so thick you can chew it and your blood runs cold, Signalis is a one-of-a-kind experience all survival horror fans need to try.

10/10  MASTERPIECE

Let me get my only criticism of this game out of the way early so I can gush a bit: I don't think the combat is particularly interesting. Survival horror doesnt need *vibrant* combat -- it probably -should- feel slow and unpleasant -- but the variety of enemies doesn't translate out to there being a whole lot of different types of fights. You'll avoid fights often not because you need to conserve resources, but because avoiding combat is significantly faster, and once you've won a four-or-five-on-one *once* it plays out the same every other time. There are a mercifully small number of boss fights. The enemies are often the least tense/scary parts of the game, so that part unraveling is a little unfortunate.

For the good: Signalis is a gorgeous, well-crafted, and thoroughly engaging survival horror game. It's not shy about what it borrows from SH and RE, nor should it be; Signalis's setting, mystery, and horror stand on their own plenty well. The UI is snappy and reserved, the controls are reasonably intuitive. There's a variety of puzzles and they can be figured out in a relatively reasonable amount of time (except for a [spoiler]water tank puzzle[/spoiler], but that's nothing new for [spoiler]water tank puzzles[/spoiler] Playtesters must have agreed, since [spoiler]it's the only puzzle with direct step-by-step instructions to solve it right next to it[/spoiler]).

The game's aesthetic is especially worth mentioning and probably a big part of why you're considering getting it to begin with. The use of sound and pared-back visuals to complement the setting's retrofuture is extremely well done. Bitcrushed audio and low-fi pixel art combine to make a wonderfully spartan ALIEN-esque tech infrastructure. Low-poly 3D models with low-res textures combine with fixed camera angles and a low render resolution to give you something that emulates the look and feel of PS1 survival horror with the smooth conveniences of something more modern.

The game's storytelling also deserves a lot of credit. The seeds of the mystery are sewn early and nurtured lovingly. There's some narrative sleight-of-hand at play that will try to mislead you about the nature of the story -- and perhaps even succeed! Its handful of cutscenes more often than not utilize a sort of music video -esque dreamy sort of quality with sporadic cuts and oppressive UI impositions that I think really spice up the specific kind of space-horror Signalis is going for.

The game also has a lot of really cool gameplay twists I won't spoil here. The radio module in particular gets more love than you might expect. I almost wish there had been more -- there are some modules like the flashlight that are used for puzzles, but in only two real ways, and a limited camera module which has no real function if you take notes outside the game at all. It'd be nice to see a future take on this game that incorporates the modules more aggressively to create even more complex puzzles.

Ultimately, if you want a cool eldritch sci-fi horror story with girls being in love and a commendable eight-hour Classic Survival Horror game attached, this is as good as it gets.

SIGNALIS is first and foremost a very riveting and exciting title. The game is geared to (and rewards) observant and methodical gameplay, though this does not make it boring by any stretch, as I personally found having the tension ratcheted up to 11 made for a far more exhilarating experience. I am not usually scared by games, but I have not felt the constant, adrenaline-spiked fear of hunting in the dark since I have played Cold Waters.

I very much enjoyed the artstyle as well. I typically play games with more realistic experiences, but SIGNALIS has achieved such a synthesis with its retro-aesthetic that I cannot imagine it being done any other way. Rose-Engine have proved that it is possible to do more with less with this title (don't forget to turn CRT-mode on!!!)

SIGNALIS is probably the most emotionally moving game I have ever played, which was a low bar, but is now very, very high. [b]Today I played:[/b]
SIGNALIS, a resident-evil-esque survival horror set in a sci-fi world.
You play as Elster, a Replika android searching for her lost crewmate and trying to figure out who and what she is. 
Then thinks get a little... [i]weird[/i]. In the lovecraftian sense. 

So, [u]gameplay[/u] first. The vast majority of the game is third person fixed camera like the old RE games. The name of the game is survival horror, with ammo in severely short supply and enemies that get back up after a while. The item to perma-kill them is [b]extremely[/b] limited, so should be saved only for the shieldbearers since they take the most ammo economy to down. [b]There is no melee weapon capable of killing enemies[/b] that I found, which makes ammo conservation the chief concern of the moment to moment gameplay. 
In this, the Inventory has [i]issues[/i]. You only have 6 inventory slots, and that's including equipped weapon, tools, and key items. On several occasions I had to backtrack to the box to drop junk so I could pick up a key item, which in turn gave the enemies time to respawn. It's vicious, and ngl at one point I totally cheated and gave myself extra perma-killers just to not have to deal with that crap. That aside, combat is easy enough - just keep your crosshair on target till you get a good shot, then hit them once or twice to knock them down, then go stomp on them to finish them off. 

Outside of combat, the puzzles are fairly straight forward - again much like old RE games, you're wandering the halls until you find both a triangle shaped keyhole and a triangle shaped object to put in it, etc. There's some more complex ones involving using your radio or recording information from elsewhere in the level, and by the end of my run I had about 4 pages in my IRL notebook of just keeping track of stuff. It was pretty fun and engaging, and not at all frustrating - aside again from backtracking to the box to pick up the particular key item needed at any given moment. 

Total first playthrough runtime was about 8.5hrs for me, and at GBP15.99 that puts me at about 2.00/hr. which isn't terrible, especially given what I'ma talk about next.
So, onto the meat of this game. Haha. Meat.

[u]Art and Audio direction[/u] is absurdly good. This is some of the sickest pixel style art I've ever seen, with lovely reflections, shadows, it's a real nice time. There's little music in the game, but plenty of ambient noise so it never felt weird. And when you tune into the slightly more cursed radio frequencies, oh boy oh boy. Lot of it's in German, though everything vital is translated of course. But still, if you happen to sprechen a little there's some fun stuff there. 
Then outside of the quality itself, just the [i]feel[/i] of it is fantastic. When you're in these trashed out living quarters, the falling apart maintenance tunnels, the meat dungeon, it all just feels great. Its grungy future-tech-meets-CRT-monitor style is absolutely reminiscent of classic horror in the best way, and I adore it.

Then we're on to [u]Story, World and Lore[/u], which is where this game shines. While wandering the world looking for the next macguffin for your macguffin shaped key hole, the world is full to the brim with environmental storytelling and notes to read. This is a +very+ reading heavy game, so turn back now if you're not into that, though I absolutely loved it. The lore snippets include the state of the solar system at war, information on Replikas and the mostly-still-humans they serve, diaries, computer logs, it's great. This world is [i]great[/i] and goddamn it I want to write something in it now.
As we progress to endgame and things get a bit more twisted (again, lovecraft time) this kinda falls away a bit, but it works well enough. I'd have preferred if they hadn't leaned quite so hard into the inexplicable, but honestly that's a minor nitpick. 

And, mentioning lovecraft, this is a [u]Horror[/u] game. No jumpscares or anything like that, it's the old school building dread and knowing this world is beyond doomed. The ending [spoiler]was a little disappointing, but fit this theme. I wasn't expecting a happy ending, but I was kinda hoping I guess?[/spoiler]. The late game areas get quite fleshy quite quick, with an appropriate number of dismembered corpses in cages, people reduced to piles of writhing meat, and doomed notes that just read "kill me kill me killmekillme". It's great!

And that about wraps up the most of it!
Oh also I didn't get the best ending, I think. Pain.

This review is going to be extremely personal, exactly like the experience SIGNALIS gives you.

You are not playing as Elster. You are Elster. You will merely see what Elster sees, and understand just as much.

By the end of the story, you're drained. Whichever ending you got, it's exactly what you deserve. Whether it's MEMORY, LEAVE or PROMISE, your fears and behavioral patterns are now exposed. It's what you've been doing your entire life, and it's exactly what you, Elster, did here. You are the lore. And once you see yourself under this light, there's no way to unsee it.

There is no true ending, no canon. No morale. Because what Rose Engine created, is not a game, but a mirror that reflects your very true self. Only question being whether you are self-reflective enough to see it.

SIGNALIS is an incredible survival horror game that is all about slow-paced, methodical exploration. There is going to be a lot of finding keys to unlock doors, a lot of reading notes, and a lot of map-checking. There will also be a good amount of scary monsters. SIGNALIS nails each of these aspects, but what really makes it stand out is its excellent presentation.

Exploration is great. It maintains being interesting throughout the game because the areas you explore are quite varied, and because, in addition to necessary items for progress, you are also always finding new clues about characters and lore as you go. The characters especially are well-written, and seeing them change over the story is a compelling reason to push forward through difficult sections.

Puzzles and enemies impede your progress along the way. The puzzles I think have wonderful flavour and dressing, but are generally weak. They're visually and thematically cool, but they are never challenging and can sometimes feel like busywork.

Thankfully enemies and combat encounters are solid. Enemy units have exquisitely gross designs with a good amount of variation. Some enemies even require you fight them in completely different ways, like with your radio, rather than conventional weapons. Even for regular enemies you can choose to shoot them, sneak by, or run past, with all options feeling equally viable.

My major nitpick of the game would be that your inventory is rather restrictive. Obviously, this is by design to force you into making tough choices. But you only have six spots and those evaporate fast:

* the flashlight is very valuable and literally required in several areas
* you'll probably want to bring a gun
* plus some ammo
* and some healing
* and you often have to carry a key item with you for a puzzle

I don't mind being tight on inventory in a survival horror, but this is too tight. I routinely had only 1 or even 0 free spaces for extra items and it eventually ceased to cause me tension and just got annoying.

But what makes SIGNALIS a truly memorable game is that everything is all wrapped up in a beautiful, unique presentation. It has so much flair and style in all aspects: the sound, music, atmosphere, characters, and mood are all gorgeous.

I love the mish-mash of various languages and cultures making up the Nation. I love the red/white/black theming that is everywhere. It's just the right amount of dark and brooding without coming across as edgy. The game depicts tragedy and the human struggle without seeming like it's trying too hard.

SIGNALIS made me fall in love with the world it crafted. Sometimes it was serene, other times it was horrifying... sombre, hopeful, tragic, or like a nightmare. But the plot and lore stuck with me and I've been thinking about it a lot. The writing is really that good.

SIGNALIS is fantastic and I give it a strong recommendation for fans of the genre. I think it's probably too hardcore for newcomers to survival horror, but there are accessibility settings if you think it's stylish enough you'd want to give it a try.

Signalis is a horror game that doesn’t scare but haunts you with grief. It is a melancholic and beautiful meditation on identity, memory, and the endurance of love in the face of erosion. In my opinion, it doesn’t simply pay homage to the classics, it sits alongside them.

Despite the obvious inspirations of Resident Evil’s fixed camera claustrophobia and the psychologic horror of Silent Hill its syntax is entirely modern, and its ambitions are literary. A masterwork of atmospheric oppression framed as a recursive descent into a nightmare.

Where many games rely on the now overused pixelated dithering and FPU-less jittering of 90s graphics as a crutch when it otherwise serves no artistic purpose, in Signalis, the denial of high-fidelity realism forces our imagination to fill in the jagged edges. The nightmares blur and so to our view of them. The art direction marries the cold, hard lines of DDR-era brutalism with the melancholic decay of a future that should never have been.

The use of color is striking. The palette is starved, dominated by oppressive greys and blacks, which makes the sudden violent intrusion of high-contrast red feel visually assaulting. That visual language is paired with an auditory landscape that is suffocating. The sound design, from the hum of fluorescent lights in the eerie quiet of a hall to the jagged breathing of Elster in the backdrop of grinding machinery creates an atmosphere that bears down with every step.

Narratively, it rejects linear clarity in favor of oneiric logic. It draws heavily on Robert Chambers’ The King in Yellow, interweaving themes of madness, memory, and recursive reality into a tragic romance between a Replika unit and her Gestalt human officer. The storytelling is fragmented, delivered through environment, cryptic radio frequencies, and sudden, jarring shifts in perspective. 

On first playthrough I could just barely piece together a string of events, the likes of which withstood no analysis without twisting on itself. While I am often critical of games that require multiple playthroughs experiencing the same material to no benefit, Signalis is one of the few that successfully avoids that pitfall with every detail serving to reify the memory of a dream. The satisfaction of its writing lies in its refusal to hold your hand: it demands distinct intellectual engagement, asking you to piece together a timeline that is actively collapsing in on itself.

While the horror the gameplay presents is a corruption of putrified viscera, the story presents one that is existential: the horror of dementia, of losing one’s self to a looping cycle of duty and failure. The central motif of ‘The Promise’ made to the woman you love anchors the cosmic abstraction in a deeply human and intimate emotional core. On first playthrough, the surrealism was confused but you realize you are experiencing their mental state. Subsequently, every flash of unreason became an exasperation of sorrow.

The puzzles are tactile and interactions outstandingly diegetic: a future of androids and space travel calling for you to tune radios, develop photos, and do basic maintenance. These are extensions of utility in a world of repression lived in by people just trying to get by. You’re grounded in the physical reality of the facility even as your metaphysical reality crumbles away.

If anybody ever asked me to give an example of a video game as an art form, this would be it. My undisputed number one choice is this game, because what it achieves in storytelling and atmosphere is unlike anything I’ve ever experienced, it just stays with you. Like all great artwork, it lingers in your mind long after you've finished it.

Never in my life have I been obsessed with something like this, and for good reason. I could talk about this game and how it makes me feel for days. I think everyone who has finished it and seen all the endings will agree: in the end, the meaning, and essentially the entire story, depends on personal interpretation. I love that about Signalis. It gives you so much while simultaneously giving you so little, leaving ample room for players to find their own meaning, to see what they wish in its story. In a narrative like this, that can mean a great deal to many people. But the central theme is unavoidable: like in life, everyone needs companionship. This is ultimately a bittersweet and tragic story of love, with a touch of cosmic horror. It’s about finding love and acceptance in the worst of circumstances, and I can’t help but adore it, even as it makes me cry every time.

Going into this game blind is pivotal, and I would give anything to be able to play it for the first time again. But because of the sheer amount of detail and the many ambiguous messages, this game is worth replaying over and over, just for the new things you notice with each playthrough, not to mention the deeper understanding of the story and timeline you gain each time. As someone who loves story-driven narrative games, this is hands down the best experience I’ve ever had, books, movies, games, any medium, there's just nothing like it.

The first time I played this game blind, it was utterly confusing, yet emotionally gripping. It immediately made me want to learn more about the game, its world, its characters, and everything in between. Afterward, I explored other, older media that were either clear or subtle inspirations for Signalis: I played through Silent Hill 2 and Nier, watched Neon Genesis Evangelion, and read some Lovecraft and The King in Yellow, which the game so prominently features. Despite all the insight I’ve gained from experiencing these works, I still appreciate Signalis the most, for how it borrows these ideas while expanding on them with its own rich world and creative vision.

The sheer amount of artwork the game incorporates is also impressive, not just because it uses it all effectively, from paintings to classical music, but because it functions like a digital gallery, a collection of different art forms across time periods presented in a unique, immersive way.

When it comes to the music that isn't borrowed, Cicada Sirens and 1000 Eyes absolutely deliver in the original soundtrack. The atmosphere is incredible, whether in the slow, sentimental tracks or the more action-packed, terror-laden ones, the music never disappoints. Another standout element is the way the game communicates its story outside of cutscenes, through the world itself, its environments, and its notes.

The dystopian world of Signalis is fascinating, partly because it might one day resemble our own, but also because of how little concrete information you're given about it and its inhabitants. That scarcity makes you pay closer attention to every detail. Some environments echo Silent Hill’s technique, presenting hellish versions of familiar places. Like the notes scattered throughout the game, they often serve as unreliable narrators. Still, whether they're explaining gameplay mechanics, puzzles, or story elements, the notes are always worth reading.

As far as gameplay goes, it does a great job of imitating old survival horror games from the early 2000s, like Resident Evil and Silent Hill, but ultimately, it's simply solid, nothing groundbreaking, but well executed. Where it truly shines is in its cryptic yet compelling storytelling, which remains brilliant down to the last detail.

The simple, low-poly visual style with a pixelated filter not only evokes a retro aesthetic that echoes the games it draws inspiration from, but also offers a distinctive lens through which to experience the story. The shifting gameplay perspectives, the varied cutscene styles, and the parallels between them create an incredibly vibrant experience, both visually and mechanically, with a satisfying mix of classic and cleverly designed new puzzles.

In conclusion, Signalis is an emotionally mature and deeply thoughtful game that explores classism and the nature of affection. Its unique visual style and gripping storytelling achieve pure terror not through typical horror conventions, but through the narrative itself. Within its genre, it’s a 10/10, without a doubt. As an indie game, I believe it surpasses most others in its class, and it's not even close. I love my space lesbians, and I’ll likely never love another game this much again.

[h1] Mind Contamination. [/h1] 

Signalis is like no other game I've played. And I do not mean that in a superficial sense; you can play a variety of games in the realm of survival horror with similar combat and puzzle mechanics. Although this game may be like several of those, including the predecessors it is inspired by that I've seen mentioned in other reviews, it is simultaneously like none of those and nothing else at all.

To me, what Signalis propagates with its being is something that exists in the realms where other-worldly love and nauseating existential horror precariously join hands as one, creating an indissoluble conglomerate of paradox. It's quite disturbing, but just as captivating and engrossing, and I believe it's because we all have these pieces within us if we search hard enough.

I am haunted by certain ideas from time to time. These ideas tend to encapsulate something that I think about quite often: the disintegration of life, of myself, of the few people I love. The decay of the body, the decay of memories and of the self that once was - the prospect of every discrete point of time in an individual's life that has existed being methodically and deliberately broken down faster and faster to a singular point of destruction, like a loose freight train whose brakes have failed, tumbling head first into its final absolution with a quickening pace. And nothing in the universe can possibly stop it: it is the ultimate truth of everything in existence, indifferent to our desires and wishes, indifferent to our suffering and our pleas.

It is the omnipotent fact that we are powerless against destruction from time itself; the idea that infects the mind like a rapidly replicating virus and never leaves you until you are finally relieved of consciousness and rotting in the ground.

As you venture through the remains of this post-dystopia Signalis presents you, ripe with environmental horrors of once living, human-like units being absorbed into the walls and floors and a space enmeshed with uncanny claustrophobia that toes the line between psychotic hallucination and cold sanity, you begin to uncover these underlying ideas of breakdown and putrefaction that will claim us all without exception.

It's in the bloodied and crumpled notes, in the unnerving cut scenes that were hacked together with dizzying imagery, conjuring subconsciously repressed perceptions, hidden intuitions, fragmented memories, aspects of reality that exist on the exterior lines of one's conscious self: Signalis presents to you the dissolution of the body and the annihilation of the mind through both the cruelty of the hands of time and through an oppressive, uncaring regime that treats the individual as nothing more than an object, a tool: a paradigm that is not far off from the one we currently exist in.

The esoteric subjects this game touches on cannot be found in many places. Enjoy your time with it, savor it and relish it, because it is a rarity, especially in its unique anime-like presentation that I found resemblances to in the art of Tsutomu Nihei with its wiry, dark, cyberhorror design.

[h1] "Remember Our Promise." [/h1] 

For all of it's darkness, all of its screeches and gore and ominous, encrypted aesthetic that permeate the fabric of your senses while you experience this unique piece of art, there is an undying desire and an unflinching love to see another person once more that carries you - the main character - onward until the end.

In the desolate and barren world that Elster finds herself in, she will stop at nothing to reach her goal. Not a missing arm, nor a shredded torso cavity exposing vital organs will prevent this from happening. She made a promise. She would once again see the one who brought her a feeling akin to happiness in the chaos of the inhumane, relentlessly hierarchical and mechanically delineated machine.

I loved how Signalis managed to interweave a romance story - a search for the other - into its bleak horror. The combination of these two things, at first glance, is an unlikely pairing. But they only reinforce each other's strengths, because it is through the misfortunes and the tragedy in our life that our bonds with others are strengthened and become that much more important, and it is through our connection with others that we feel that we can gather more strength to face the dismal environment that has cared for us not once. Sometimes, you simply need something else - or someone else - to carry onward.

With few words and sparing, minimalist imagery, Signalis let's you catch a glimpse of the mysterious, melancholy-laden story of Elster and her companion, and their relationship to the futile world they inhabit.

[h1] Hidden gem compartmentalized. [/h1] 

Signalis has everything I could ask for.  Survival horror.  Aesthetic.  Melancholy.  Obfuscation.  Anime.  Distorted and questionable perceptions that may not correspond to reality.  The deleterious effect of oppressive regimes on the psyche.

Although there were times that I felt the combat to be clunky, or times where I was kind of annoyed that I had to backtrack again and trigger the same sounds and soundtrack from the monsters, I enjoyed every minute of Signalis.  I knew I would enjoy it from the moment I booted it up and saw (and listened to) the menu screen. Stern’s answer caught my attention and I admit throughout my time playing games with multiple outcomes in the finale. I realize I am guilty of this too. And yet, this establishes a thought-provoking notion to provide clarification, evidence, and reasoning, beyond simple claims. Player interpretation differs for each individual. Classified as neither good, bad, or in between. It simply is. Consensus can say comparable beginnings, middle, and end. And yet, we conjure causes to describe something that can be difficult or perhaps easy to comprehend. In my attempt to understand everything throughout my playthrough, I’ve come to see it as a Lovecraftian Sci-Fi blended with Survival Horror. Reputable individuals have noted inspiration, references, and homages to King in Yellow by Robert W. Chambers. The Festival by H.P. Lovecraft. Evangelion by Hideaki Anno, Stanley Kubrick, Resident Evil & Silent Hill franchise Et al. To me, include Nier and Prey(2017). With a dash of Studio Shaft’s techniques. And while I haven’t read/watched/played some of those homages they harken too. A considerable amount of careful effort to not create a reference-filled fiesta akin to Ready Player One. You control Elster, a [Redacted] in search of someone important to her. This is her journey after her ship crashes onto an unknown planet. She doesn’t start with much, but a sufficient tutorial resides to grant a fighting chance. Make no mistake, this isn’t a game you run away from consistently. You. Can. Fight. Back. From a top-down 2.5D perspective. Lengthwise, the game took me over nine hours to complete and I didn’t have any major/minor bugs or crashes. Ran smoothly notwithstanding looking akin to a Playstation One game. An aesthetic remarkably familiar to our past of CRTs, floppy discs, and VCRs with unfamiliar technology. A retro-tech meets dystopian surrealism. An unforgiving world, which I became horrified to learn about and lost myself in admiring the art. A pleasant strength tied to supplementary elements the game displays to the player. 

The combat felt very tight, responsive and didn’t suffocate me constantly. For several moments I would have despaired, but a handy walkthrough and some tips kept my spirits up! Outside of combat. I found worldbuilding to be richly rewarding and added substance to the environmental storytelling. I was [b]craving[/b] to know more about the inhabitants, the government, the leaders, technology, etc. Missions and roles for each [R$%#%$#@] unit and even enemies are spared no expense in displaying how they came to be. Thereby, making recollections of pertinent details at the press of a button, straightforward.

This game will be a classic.  It's an excellent ode to survival horror of generations past, weird fiction, lovecraftian horror, and existentialist manga and anime.  It's a powerful experience that is best to go into unspoiled.  

The gameplay systems here work together very well.   Playing as a Replika, a sort of biomechanical clone of a human, your UI is all part of your programming.  So are its limitations.  The games UI is an unsung hero of the gameplay, as little tweaks drastically impact how you must play the game.  You are only allowed 6 inventory slots, which means you're going to have to plan what you carry, where, and when.  With most of the gameplay involving carrying, combining and interacting with key items to solve puzzles, each level becomes a puzzle box in of itself.  

You will slowly unveil each level, and eventually the keys and components within will start to make sense to you.  Once you have an idea of how to solve the puzzles at hand, the execution of solving them is still a challenge, as you must contend with enemies who stalk the narrow hallways of your descent into hell.

For me, the most appealing part about a horror story is the element of mystery.  There is something beyond our human understanding, interrupting our lives.  During your first few hours, nothing about the story will make sense.  This is where I think the story could've jumped the shark.  If it were all some metaphor, some beautiful indie "it was all a dream" type thing, I would've been pissed.  Thankfully, there is an actual story here, and while the lines between dream and reality are blurred, there is a deeply rewarding, lore-rich explanation for this.  It drip-feeds you enough information to piece the story together for yourself without giving you all the answers.  It's a compelling mystery, with a devastatingly beautiful core.

I think Signalis might be one of my new favourite games ever.  Any of its individual influences may not be for everyone, but as a package, it transcends its roots and demands to be played.  Please try.

SIGNALIS wears its MANY direct inspirations on its sleeve - it combines, AMONG OTHERS, many notable pieces of 90s-00s Japanese anime and gamer culture with Lovecraftian horror literature and a broader European 19th-20th century cultural (classical art and music) and historical influence that creates a both unique and familiar artistic experience - for that alone, it deserves attention. A major scene includes a direct scene reference to Ghost in the Shell (1995), interspersed with images directly referencing Neon Genesis Evangelion, while the track 'Die Toteninsel' plays - which is a reference to the series of paintings of the same name (Böcklin, 1880s) which  features heavily in the scene (and the rest of the game) as well, but it is itself inspired by Rachmaninoff's piece of the same name, itself based on one of the paintings. This will either annoy you, or it will make you feel very cultured - I'm not sure which of those I am. 
After I first played it, I spent about a month trying to understand it - suffice to say, I am very invested in SIGNALIS - it's definitely my favorite game so far. It seems it inspired a new wave of indie titles, so here's hoping we'll get a similar banger in the future! <3

[h1] Welcome to my review of SIGNALIS [/h1]

[b]TL:DR if you're too lazy to read; very good game and you should buy it, YES at full price. But not if you're a gooner, don't let the tourists give you a false impression about the setting and characters.[/b]

[b]The Game[/b]
SIGNALIS is a game that can be summarised as "PS2 graphics RE clone". But that's not very fair because it does so much more than just that. While it certainly borrows a lot from the older resident evil games, it still stands out from it not only because of the setting, but also the general feel. Unlike those older games, it feels much more responsive while sacrificing nothing when it comes to visuals. I really don't have much to put here for gameplay. It plays well, the puzzles don't feel unfair and I didn't feel like the game was ever being unfair, even during the boss fights. That said, the survival difficulty IS REALLY, HARD. I'm going to gloat and say I did beat it on survival difficulty but man what a slog. Was worth it though, got the secret/true ending that way. The game is very optimized and doesn't require crazy hardware to run. I also encountered no bugs at all, atleast none that I could remember so theres that too!

[b]The Setting.[/b]
Needless to say, the character design and setting are sublime! While there are many games and shows I've played and seen throughout my life, this game has one of the best I've ever seen and I mean that wholeheartedly. Humanity builds a space empire ruled by a corrupt religious order, which then spawns a communist rebellion that fights back against the order. Many years pass the war drags on, the communists having the upper hand. The brutality and need to win spawns a new super weapon, the Replika. Robotic humans that seem more human at first glance, but are very mechanical underneath. Very brutally purposeful to their intended role, and just as disposable if disobedient. These robo-humans are stunning in their design and implementation. Cogs in an oppressive machine, doing as their told while trying to make something out of their existence. The communist Super state of the "Eusan Nation" is a offshoot of the former GDR/DDR but if they were in space. The fact that they can basically make a super humans, but other technology has stagnated somewhere around the early 90's is so interesting and so cool to see. Cute little robo-girls that can be the thought police but still carry around weapons designed in 70's is just- Something I don't know how describe but I just love them. Even the humans look so cool in this game. The bread and butter are the Replika's though. My personal favourite is the Kolibri or KLBR.

[b]STORY[/b]
[spoiler] Arianne, your girlfriend, is dying. How did we get here? Well Arianne is not like the other girls. She hasn't accepted the fact she is another cog in the machine of war and status quo. Arianne is who she wants to be, and artist, a free spirit. This is not good enough, the state knows something she doesn't and therefor she has been sent on a mission. Go beyond our milky way, find new life, find a new beginning. You will accompany her on this journey, LSTR-512. You get to know Arianne, and you two eventually start falling in love. Thing is though, this mission was a one way trip. Arianne was meant to die, and you as a disposable replika, were meant to die with her. Arianne knows the writing is on the wall, and needs you to finish her off before the ship fully fails after so long in space. Thing is, that thing the government knew about has come back to bite you and Arianne hard, and it is unknown if she other got back the powers that be. As you see, Arianne is not a normal girl, she has natural bio-resonance. Minds so powerful that they can alter space and time around them. And now, in Arianne's dying moments, you are forever trapped with her, trying to break the cycle. Other have been ripped from their reality to bask in Arianne's agony, much against their will. You will endless roam her memories of how she saw the world around her, mindless monsters attacking her everywhere she went, and faint moments of self-expression, corrupted and repressed. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] In your first play through, you will get one of three endings, all of which are the "false bad ending". Some are less worse than others, but the outcome is the same, you are doomed to repeat cycle. I must also address the fake-out ending half way through the game, that really hit hard and was the few times I've cried at a story and game in recent memory. The true ending is the "Artifact" ending, and the one I strongly believe to be canon. This does require a second play through. Trust me though, its worth it. You can finally break the cycle in one last happy memory. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] There are 3 total chapters in this game each divided into sub-chapters. Chapter 1 is the strongest in my opinion and all of the sub-chatpers are really good too. Eases you into the setting and gameplay in a interesting fun way. Chapter 2 is- well I think in this case we have to talk about the sub-chapters. Part 7: Excavation is a strong part of this chapter but its only downside is that it is very short. Part 8: Nowhere, was the low point in the game. While the horror themes were strongest and most interesting, the gameplay in this part of the game felt very tedious and is such a slog to get through.
