I think an issue with modern horror games is that they seem to lack identity, typically falling under the modern misconception that realism is the best way to immerse players. On the other hand, [b]SIGNALIS is a game that is simply brimming with identity[/b], seeking to convey a story with a mixture of elements that create a memorable experience by not compromising itself with realism, but instead embraces creativity without limit. Never have I thought that we needed a sci-fi horror with lovecraftian-esque themes, and yet this game exists and managed to pull it off well. 

Gameplay-wise, it's fairly simplistic, clearly inspired by retro horror games such as RE1 and Silent Hill. Yet, the contents of the game itself is bountiful, from the levels you traverse through to the tidbits of lore you stumble upon, and maintains its own entire identity separate from the games that inspired it. The world of SIGNALIS is unique and very much horrifying, keeping the information of the world you're in such an enigmatic way, yet is rich enough to give you a sense of what is happening, leaving you ponder about the gaps in information deliberately left behind. Not to mention the build up to the insanity of it all, constantly putting me in a state of awe to what I got myself into. I can't stress enough how well is this game's presentation.

I'm fairly certain that this game is the inspiration for all the subsequent decent indie horror games that have been releasing in the past few years. That being said, [b]SIGNALIS is certainly one of the best examples of what a horror game should be.[/b]

Seeing the amount of positive reviews this is getting makes me sad to leave a negative review, especially given that I've been looking forward to this game for a very long time now, but sadly the things I don't like are just outweighing the things I do. 

So, for those that are unaware this is a horror game that gameplay wise tries to emulate the old Silent Hill and Resident Evil games, where you had limited inventory space, engaging in combat was a deliberate, risky decision, etc. This game basically follows that formula, meaning you get limited healing items, ammunition, etc. that you have to make the conscious choice of when to use. However, this game has some issues with this system that made it a much more frustrating experience for me than anything else.

The first main issue is the limit on your inventory space. You only have 6 slots of inventory space, which your weapon, ammo, healing items, etc. will take up. This, for me, is all fine. What's not fine is the fact that all of the story related items you find (aka keycards and such) *also* take up space in your inventory. Even in the time that I played the game, I had already experienced multiple points of frustration where I completed a puzzle and went to pick up the item(s) from the puzzle, only to realize my inventory was full and I had to backtrack to store some stuff. Even worse are the modules. For reference, your character in this game is an android. You would think that these modules, such as a special eyeball that can take pictures or a chest-mounted flashlight, would be extra functionalities permanently unlocked with their own button, right? Wrong. These modules also *take up inventory space*, and the flashlight looked like it was going to be close to necessary for exploration purposes (I quit roughly around the point you get that), meaning you'd essentially be permanently down an inventory slot if you didn't wanna get caught off guard by unlit rooms.

Compounded on top of this was an already frustrating tendency I was seeing to just spam multiple enemies in tight rooms or corridors. To me, don't make combat such a last resort decision and ammo/healing items so scarce if you're going to put multiple enemies in rooms and hallways such that it's hard to avoid them without taking damage. All that's going to want to make me do is save scum if I take too much damage because I know if I use too much ammo or healing now I might get fucked later. Even worse is the fact that enemies don't stay dead once you put them down. Eventually, enemies will just get back up as if nothing happened, unless you used thermite flares on their bodies to destroy their organic components. Not only does this disincentivize combat even further, because why would you put down enemies if you aren't going to finish the job with thermite, it also means you're almost never going to want to actually use the damn thermite because that too is a limited resource you have to use for "the right moment".

Don't get me wrong, there are definitely good qualities about this game. The art direction is quite good, I like the PS1 style in the full 3D sections, the puzzles that I ran into all made sense, I'm intrigued by what actually happened in the game world and want answers to all my questions about the lore and story. But the sad part is, all of that is bogged down by the absolute tedium that is actually engaging with the gameplay, when the design and enemy placement is what it is. This tedium also detracts from the fact that this is supposed to be a horror game. When I first booted up the game, I was a bit unnerved and super excited to see where they were going to take it. However, in just a few hours that tenseness and edge of my seat feeling just turned into frustration when I ran into yet another hallway with multiple enemies tactically positioned to gank you from multiple angles.

Overall, I'm just disappointed with this game more than anything I think. I've had my eye on it for at least a year, and the trailers hit every single note they needed to hit, but the game is just too annoying to play. If you don't mind save scumming to save on resources and figure out what the best path to traverse the levels is, and don't mind having to constantly run around pairs or trios of enemies, then you'll probably enjoy this game, but I just don't see how that's good design honestly.
If I could play a game again for the first time this would be the game. Words cannot do this masterpiece enough justice.

Signalis is a modern old school game that takes notes from survival horror and literature classics such as Resident Evil, Silent Hill, a bit of Dead Space, Blame!, Evangelion, the works of HP Lovecraft, and Robert W. Chambers. It takes pieces and parts from all of them to make a fun and memorable tribute game while having an identity all its own.

It's made to play like an "older" game with its gameplay quirks and presentation, but under all of that is a memorable survival game that touches on love, regrets, the horror of the unknown, to live with the acceptance of helplessness, and the clawing madness of wanting answers to where there is none.

What I like:
-A good mix of action, sci-fi, and psychological horror.
-A churning story and premise that makes the imagination go wild the more I played.
-Easy and Normal mode can let you get away with a lot of things.
-Can run on old or low speced machines well.
-Its style. 90s styled computer graphics mixed with Cold War inspired pieces, Eurasian influences, and anime art.
-Combat is simple, but the game restricting you to one stack of ammo, resurrecting enemies, and a stomp gives strategic weight to every encounter. Do you risk getting in close to save ammo? Is this enemy worth fighting in the long run?
-A parry shove mechanic that makes running and exploration less stressful. 
-Health is partially restored when saving the game and has limited health regen.
-Open ended interpretations of the story. It's as simple or complicated as you want it to be!
-Tries to be "meta" or self-aware and reflects your gameplay style to tie in with certain themes.
-The game is very subtly heavyhanded about its references: It uses quotes from the books its inspired by, the musical choices, and even a warning from real life quoted almost word for word! It's almost funny.
-A cursor appears on items if you're close to them.
-Variable difficulty and optional QoL choices such as holding more items.
-Levels are small enough that they're easy to traverse and backtrack.
-All of of the puzzles offer hints through messages and notes.
-Focuses more on ammo management, which is a neat twist to the genre. Health is free, but you pay for your life with bullets!
-The music is very atmospheric and runs a wild gamut of classical, atonal sine wave ambience, to tense, to gritty bit crunched industrial.

What I didn't like:
-Picking up items still makes you vulnerable and enemies can attack you out of it.
-No grace period when entering a room. I've taken damage or even died a few times because I ran right into an enemy after going through a door. It's a rare occurrence but can feel cheap at times.
-No gallery to view artwork or replay endings
-Free Aim (Tab) is near useless without a mouse because the laser pointer is too small to see.
-Aiming with a controller can be very tricky due to the default lock-on aiming mode.
-Very slow first person panning with a controller, which makes turning and observing objects annoying.
-Sound mixing is all over the place on certain sound setups. Gun fire and menu sounds can be abnormally loud, music can sound muffled, opening doors can be too quiet.
-Parry shove while holding a firearm is only possible if you're aiming down the weapon. 
-Some key items and important spots blend in with the background too well. 
-Item management is a pain in its default state.
-Item placement and distribution could have been better.
-Navigating the menus can get tedious.
-You can only pick up items found in the field. You can't use them immediately or combine them with items in your inventory. (Why can Elster only use items that are in her bag. Is she stupid? jkjk)
-Rigid map: The game doesn't let you know once a room is fully looted or doesn't say what key you need to open a door.
-Running out of ammo for bosses.
-Some of its references and metaphors are too on the nose however. Where does the homage end, and the real meaning begin? It's cool and mysterious if you don't know, but it's as subtle as an airhorn if you know!
-Piecing the lore and parts of the story together can be very overwhelming.

Lastly! To any new comers, the "Sesbian Lex" memes are from the community. I know we can be silly at times, but the game is consistently serious throughout so don't worry about tonal whiplash while playing ^^'

What makes me sad about Signalis is that it has some legitimately good, original ideas. It just struggles with the line between paying homage to its influences and directly restating them. Unfortunately, it goes way too far over that line.

It has a very cool sci fi  setting, with some very cool deep lore, and does a lot of extremely abstract things on par with David Lynch, or  End of Evangelion, or whatever. I was impressed with the abstract storytelling, and I was looking forward to wrapping my head around it. It would be an interesting story to analyze, if not for how much time the game spends emulating Resident Evil/Silent Hill and making constant shameless references to them.

The gameplay is a blend of the old-school entries from those series: Managing resources & inventory space, exploring, moving key items from one place to another to solve a map-wide puzzle, planning which routes you'll prioritize and which enemies you'll take out to conserve resources, inspecting and rotating all the key items, etc. 

If it was just emulating them, I wouldn't be so annoyed, but it just spends way too much time referencing Silent Hill. It lifts entire scenes from Silent Hill games and shamelessly point-for-point recreates things. An amnesiac unreliable narrator looking for dead wife, weird reality-bending events surrounding the relationship to dead wife and the search for her, a copy/paste of Angela Orosco, a copy/paste of Abstract Daddy boss fight complete with Angela in the room and the walls are skin, a copy/paste of Incubus boss fight, copy/paste red save system, copy/paste mandarin, etc. ... 

Copy/paste a huge, red-tinted, non-euclidean area where your map no longer works and the save system calls it “nowhere”... I said to myself, “I recognize this reference. I am having fun right now playing Silent Hill 1.” 

Having said all that, it's an indie title so maybe cut them some slack. I don't know. They have some extremely good ideas, and it's well-polished. The ideas are just buried in a mountain of “Do you remember Silent Hill?” and rehashed gameplay from Resident Evil. If you can look past all that there's definitely something cool here but it was waaay too much for me.
